body:
The gaseous envelope of the Earth

The atmosphere is the envelope of gases surrounding the Earth and held in place by its gravitational attraction. It contains the gases necessary for life, protects the Earth's surface from harmful solar radiation, regulates temperature and provides the medium in which weather phenomena occur.

The atmosphere consists of gases, water vapour and suspended particles. Its composition is relatively uniform in the lower atmosphere when water vapour and other variable constituents are excluded.

Composition of dry air

Dry air means atmospheric air excluding water vapour. Its principal constituents, expressed as approximate percentages by volume, are as follows:

GasApproximate proportionImportance
Nitrogen (N2)78.08%Nitrogen cycle and biological growth
Oxygen (O2)20.95%Respiration and combustion
Argon (Ar)0.93%Inert atmospheric gas
Carbon dioxide (CO2)About 0.04%Photosynthesis and greenhouse effect
Other trace gasesVery small quantitiesVarious atmospheric processes

Other atmospheric gases include neon, helium, krypton, xenon, hydrogen, methane, nitrous oxide and ozone. The concentration of carbon dioxide varies over time; 0.04% is a rounded educational value, not an exact contemporary measurement.

Nitrogen and oxygen together constitute approximately 99% of dry atmospheric air by volume. Argon is the third most abundant gas, followed by carbon dioxide.

Functions of the major gases

Nitrogen

Nitrogen is essential for the formation of proteins and other biological compounds. Most plants cannot directly use atmospheric nitrogen. Nitrogen-fixing microorganisms convert it into compounds that can enter biological systems. Nitrogen also dilutes atmospheric oxygen and limits the intensity of combustion.

Oxygen

Oxygen is essential for aerobic respiration and supports ordinary combustion. It is released during photosynthesis by plants, algae and certain microorganisms.

Argon

Argon is a noble gas that is chemically unreactive under ordinary atmospheric conditions. Although it is much more abundant than carbon dioxide, it does not play a comparable role in the greenhouse effect.

Carbon dioxide

Carbon dioxide is used in photosynthesis and released through respiration, decomposition, volcanic activity and the burning of carbon-containing fuels. It absorbs and emits infrared radiation and contributes to the greenhouse effect.

A gas does not need to be abundant to have an important effect on climate. Carbon dioxide and ozone are examples of gases whose atmospheric significance is much greater than their small concentrations might suggest.

Atmospheric pressure and density

Gravity concentrates atmospheric gases near the Earth's surface. The weight of the overlying air produces atmospheric pressure. As altitude increases, there is less air above a particular point, so pressure generally decreases. Atmospheric density also generally decreases with height.

At high altitudes, breathing becomes more difficult because oxygen partial pressure decreases, even though the percentage of oxygen in the well-mixed lower atmosphere remains approximately the same.

Weather and climate

Weather describes atmospheric conditions at a particular place and time. Climate describes the long-term pattern and variability of weather conditions in a region, commonly assessed over periods of 30 years. Temperature, humidity, atmospheric pressure, wind and precipitation are important elements of both.

Prelims focus

  • Nitrogen is the most abundant atmospheric gas.
  • Oxygen is the second most abundant gas.
  • Argon is more abundant than carbon dioxide.
  • Atmospheric pressure and density generally decrease with altitude.
  • Trap: The most abundant atmospheric gases are not necessarily the most important greenhouse gases.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, reprint 2025–26, Chapter 7, Composition and Structure of Atmosphere, pp. 64–66; NCERT, Class 7, Our Environment, 2018–19, Chapter 4, Air, pp. 20–24; NSF NCAR Center for Science Education, What's in the Air?, consulted 28 November 2026.]

body:
Variable constituents of the atmosphere

Unlike nitrogen and oxygen, some atmospheric constituents vary considerably from one place to another and from one time to another. Water vapour and suspended particles are particularly important because they influence weather, visibility, cloud formation and the Earth's energy balance.

Water vapour

Water vapour is water in its gaseous state. It enters the atmosphere mainly through evaporation from oceans, rivers, lakes and moist surfaces, and through transpiration from vegetation.

Its proportion varies from nearly 0% to approximately 4% by volume. Warm and humid regions generally contain more water vapour than cold or dry regions. Most atmospheric water vapour is concentrated in the lower atmosphere because its main sources are near the Earth's surface.

Water vapour generally decreases from the equatorial regions towards the poles and with increasing altitude. However, local conditions, atmospheric circulation and moisture availability can modify this general pattern.

Importance of water vapour

  • It provides the moisture necessary for the formation of clouds, fog, dew and precipitation.
  • It absorbs and emits infrared radiation and is a major natural greenhouse gas.
  • Evaporation absorbs energy, while condensation releases latent heat into the atmosphere.
  • It influences atmospheric stability, cloud development and weather systems.

Water vapour is invisible. Visible clouds and fog consist mainly of tiny liquid water droplets or ice crystals, not visible water vapour.

Atmospheric aerosols

Aerosols are small solid particles or liquid droplets suspended in the atmosphere. They originate from natural processes as well as human activities.

Natural sourcesHuman-related sources
Sea salt from ocean spraySoot from fuel combustion
Mineral dust from dry landIndustrial particulate emissions
Volcanic ash and sulfate particlesSulfate particles formed from emitted gases
Pollen and natural smokeSmoke from biomass and waste burning

Aerosols are usually concentrated in the lower atmosphere, although winds, strong convection and volcanic eruptions can transport them to much greater heights.

Role of aerosols in cloud formation

As moist air cools sufficiently, water vapour can condense on suitable suspended particles. Such particles are called cloud condensation nuclei. Hygroscopic particles, such as sea salt, readily attract water and assist the formation of cloud droplets.

The presence of particles alone does not guarantee cloud formation. Adequate moisture and suitable cooling conditions are also necessary.

Effect on incoming radiation and temperature

Atmospheric particles interact with incoming sunlight in different ways. Sulfate aerosols commonly scatter solar radiation and can reduce the amount of energy absorbed by the Earth's surface. Black carbon, a component of soot, absorbs radiation and can warm the surrounding atmosphere.

Aerosols can also influence cloud properties and visibility. Consequently, their overall climatic effect depends on their composition, concentration, location and interaction with clouds. It is incorrect to assume that every aerosol produces cooling.

Scattering of sunlight

Air molecules scatter shorter visible wavelengths more strongly than longer wavelengths. This explains the predominantly blue appearance of a clear daytime sky. At sunrise and sunset, sunlight travels through a longer atmospheric path, and much of its shorter-wavelength light is scattered away, producing reddish or orange colours.

Larger aerosol particles can contribute to haze and modify these colours.

Prelims focus

  • Atmospheric water vapour commonly varies between nearly 0% and 4% by volume.
  • Water vapour generally decreases with increasing altitude.
  • Aerosols include both suspended solid particles and liquid droplets.
  • Suitable dust and sea salt particles act as condensation nuclei.
  • Trap: Some aerosols scatter sunlight, whereas others, such as black carbon, absorb it.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, reprint 2025–26, Chapter 7, Water Vapour and Dust Particles, pp. 64–65; Chapter 8, reprint 2026–27, The Passage of Solar Radiation through the Atmosphere, p. 68; NASA Earth Observatory, Aerosols: Tiny Particles, Big Impact, consulted 28 November 2026.]

title: Water Vapour, Dust and Atmospheric Aerosols

body:
Basis of atmospheric classification

The atmosphere is divided into layers mainly according to the way temperature changes with altitude. From the Earth's surface upwards, the 5 principal layers are the troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere.

The boundary heights are approximate because atmospheric conditions vary with latitude, season and solar activity.

Troposphere

The troposphere is the lowest atmospheric layer and is in direct contact with the Earth's surface. Its average upper boundary is approximately 13 km above the surface. It extends to about 8 km near the poles and about 16–18 km over equatorial regions.

Strong heating and convection in tropical regions transport air and heat to greater heights, making the tropical troposphere thicker than the polar troposphere.

The troposphere contains approximately three-fourths of the atmospheric mass and most atmospheric water vapour and aerosols. Almost all ordinary weather phenomena, including rainfall, thunderstorms, fog and most clouds, occur within it.

Temperature generally decreases with altitude in the troposphere. The standard average environmental lapse rate is approximately 6.5°C per kilometre, although actual atmospheric conditions may differ.

Tropopause

The tropopause is the transition between the troposphere and the stratosphere. It limits most tropospheric vertical mixing and is characterised by a marked change in the vertical temperature trend.

The tropical tropopause is generally higher and colder than the polar tropopause. Approximate textbook values are −80°C over the equator and −45°C over the poles. These are representative values rather than fixed temperatures.

Stratosphere

The stratosphere extends from the tropopause to approximately 50 km above the Earth's surface. Temperature generally increases with altitude through much of this layer because ozone absorbs solar ultraviolet radiation.

The relatively stable temperature structure restricts strong vertical convection. The stratosphere therefore contains comparatively little water vapour and experiences much less ordinary weather activity than the troposphere.

Commercial aircraft commonly cruise in the upper troposphere or lower stratosphere, depending on their operating altitude and the height of the tropopause. The upper boundary of the stratosphere is called the stratopause.

Mesosphere

The mesosphere extends from approximately 50 km to about 80–85 km. Temperature decreases with increasing altitude because this region receives relatively little radiative heating.

Many incoming meteoroids produce visible meteors and lose material in this layer. The mesopause, its upper boundary, is generally the coldest region of the atmosphere, with temperatures that can approach −90°C or lower.

Thermosphere

The thermosphere begins above the mesopause and extends several hundred kilometres above the Earth's surface. Temperature increases substantially with altitude because sparse atmospheric particles absorb high-energy ultraviolet radiation and X-rays from the Sun.

Although particle temperatures can be very high, the air is extremely thin. Such a high temperature does not imply the same heating effect that dense hot air near the Earth's surface would produce.

Most auroral emissions occur within the thermosphere. The International Space Station also orbits within this broad atmospheric region.

Exosphere

The exosphere is the outermost atmospheric region. Its lower boundary is often placed near 600 km, although it varies considerably. It gradually merges into outer space rather than ending at a sharp boundary.

Hydrogen and helium are important constituents of this extremely rarefied region. Some particles possess sufficient energy to escape the Earth's gravitational attraction.

Atmospheric pressure and density generally decrease upwards, but atmospheric temperature does not decrease continuously. The temperature trend alternates through the troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere and thermosphere.

Prelims focus

  • Troposphere: temperature generally decreases with altitude; most weather occurs here.
  • Stratosphere: temperature generally increases with altitude; contains most atmospheric ozone.
  • Mesosphere: temperature decreases with altitude; meteors commonly occur here.
  • Thermosphere: temperature increases with altitude; associated with auroras.
  • Exosphere: outermost, extremely rarefied atmospheric region.
  • Trap: The tropical tropopause is generally higher and colder than the polar tropopause.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, reprint 2025–26, Chapter 7, Structure of the Atmosphere, pp. 65–66, Figure 7.1; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, reprint 2020, Chapter 8, Atmosphere, pp. 54–61; NASA Science, Earth's Atmosphere: A Multi-layered Cake, consulted 28 November 2026.]

body:
Ozone as an atmospheric constituent

Ozone (O3) is a form of oxygen consisting of 3 oxygen atoms in each molecule. Ordinary molecular oxygen (O2) contains 2 oxygen atoms.

Although ozone occurs only in small quantities, it performs important atmospheric functions. Approximately 90% of atmospheric ozone is found in the stratosphere, with much of the ozone layer concentrated between approximately 15 and 35 km above the Earth's surface.

The ozone layer is not a separate thermal layer of the atmosphere. It is a region of relatively high ozone concentration within the stratosphere.

Absorption of ultraviolet radiation

Solar radiation contains ultraviolet radiation, which has shorter wavelengths than visible light. Exposure to excessive ultraviolet radiation can damage biological tissues.

Atmospheric oxygen and ozone absorb virtually all incoming UV-C radiation. Stratospheric ozone also absorbs most harmful UV-B radiation, while much of the UV-A radiation reaches the Earth's surface.

By absorbing ultraviolet radiation, ozone protects living organisms and also heats the stratosphere. This absorption explains why temperature generally increases with altitude in much of the stratosphere.

Stratospheric ozone and tropospheric ozone

The environmental effect of ozone depends strongly on its location.

FeatureStratospheric ozoneGround-level ozone
LocationStratosphereLower troposphere
Main significanceAbsorption of harmful UV radiationAir pollution
Biological effectProtects organisms from excessive UV exposureCan damage lungs and vegetation

Ground-level ozone forms mainly through chemical reactions involving nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds in the presence of sunlight. It is an important constituent of photochemical smog and also acts as a greenhouse gas.

Ozone is beneficial in the stratosphere but harmful when present at excessive concentrations near the ground. The molecule is the same; its atmospheric location determines its major effects.

The ionosphere

The ionosphere is a region of the upper atmosphere containing significant concentrations of electrically charged particles, including ions and free electrons. Solar ultraviolet radiation and X-rays produce these particles by ionising atmospheric gases.

The ionosphere overlaps the upper mesosphere and thermosphere and can extend to still greater heights. Its boundaries vary with solar activity and the time of day.

Unlike the troposphere or stratosphere, the ionosphere is defined primarily by electrical properties rather than by temperature trends. It is therefore not an additional layer in the standard sequence of 5 thermal layers.

Radio communication

Certain radio waves, particularly shortwave or high-frequency radio waves, can be refracted back towards the Earth's surface by the ionosphere. This allows communication over distances beyond the direct line of sight.

Not all radio waves behave in the same way. Some frequencies pass through the ionosphere and are used for satellite communication.

Auroras

Auroras occur when energetic charged particles interact with atmospheric gases in the upper atmosphere, causing them to emit light. They occur mainly at high latitudes because the Earth's magnetic field guides many charged particles towards polar regions.

The luminous phenomena are known as the aurora borealis in the Northern Hemisphere and aurora australis in the Southern Hemisphere.

Prelims focus

  • Ozone has the molecular formula O3.
  • Approximately 90% of atmospheric ozone occurs in the stratosphere.
  • Ozone absorption of ultraviolet radiation heats the stratosphere.
  • Ground-level ozone is an important photochemical pollutant.
  • The ionosphere assists certain forms of long-distance radio communication.
  • Trap: The ozone layer and ionosphere are not separate members of the 5-layer thermal classification.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, reprint 2025–26, Chapter 7, pp. 64–66; UNEP Ozone Secretariat, Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion: 2022, 20 Questions and Answers, Questions 1 and 2; NASA Science, Earth's Atmosphere: A Multi-layered Cake; US EPA, Ground-level Ozone Basics, online sources consulted 28 November 2026.]
